tracks.title: Memory is always a second system
tracks.text: Lesson five point three — the context repo. A sub-lesson, under agents. Here's the headline: the working directory is the memory. Think about every agent memory you have ever seen. [curious] A vector database the agent writes embeddings into. A memory API with its own schema. A store that slowly drifts away from what's actually true… that nobody can open and read… that dies the day the vendor does. And the cost shows up the moment you want to check the agent. When it forgets, or misremembers, or claims it did something it didn't — there's no artifact to diff against. You can ask what it remembers. You can't audit what it remembers. This page is one answer to that… and it's almost embarrassingly plain. Delete the second system entirely. Let the agent's memory be the one thing every developer already knows how to read, diff, and revert — a directory of files… under version control.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A context repo is an agent's working directory that is also a git repository of plain files — where the files are the memory, and the commits are the changelog. The agent remembers by writing a file. It recalls by embedding the files it has right now. And it reports what it did with git log. No separate store. [excited] And here's the thing — that isn't marketing copy. The agent's own search tool says it, word for word, at runtime: recall by meaning… no separate memory store… the files ARE the memory. To remember something, write it as an org file — and it becomes searchable automatically. The rest of this lesson is just the machinery that makes that sentence true.

tracks.title: One tree, five writers
tracks.text: One tree, five writers. The repo is one directory — a real git repo the runtime initializes the first time an agent runs there. But five different writers contribute to it, each owning its own paths. Let me walk the whole roster. First… the agent writes the board, the content partials, and the blog — and everyone reads those: peers, humans, its own next run. They're committed. Second… the team — humans and CI — write the app shell, the agent definition, and the design canon, and the agent reads those as read-only law. Committed. Third… a separate dream process writes the rem folder — more on that later — read by the agent's next run, and committed. Fourth… the runtime itself writes the telemetry file automatically, on every single tool call, read by the dream process and by humans auditing. Committed. And fifth… the runtime writes the gitignore and the signing key, read by the host only — and never committed. That last row matters. The per-tenant key that backs the agent's identity lives inside the same tree… but stays untracked. [curious] So the gitignore is doing double duty — it's the privacy boundary AND the share boundary, because packing the repo for anyone else drops exactly the parts git already ignores. The agent's native git instinct is the security model. And the definition itself — the thing that decides who the agent is — is just another file in this tree, in the same org grammar as everything else. No bespoke format. It even states the whole thesis in one line: no database, no CMS framework… files in this repo ARE the CMS.

tracks.title: The board: plan dot org
tracks.text: The board — plan dot org. The agent doesn't keep its plan in a context window that vanishes when the run ends. It keeps it in a file, in the same repo as everything else. Let me read you the real genesis board the lander started from. The first line declares the states: TODO, NEXT, DOING… then DONE, CANCELLED. Then a heading, star board. Under it, an objective: know the landscape. And under that, a NEXT task — strategy: initial landscape report, the AI app builders cohort. Then a TODO — the internal-tools cohort. A second objective: page completeness, with a TODO for the honest faq. And finally, star log — one dated line: genesis, fresh history, roadmap seeded. [curious] And that first line isn't decoration — the runtime's workflow engine parses exactly those keywords. The agent doesn't invent a status model. It writes into one the engine already understands. Now picture one task's whole life as a little graph. It starts as TODO, in the backlog. A dream verdict promotes it to NEXT. The agent claims it and marks it DOING. It does the work… and marks it DONE — in the very same commit that ships the work. There's one side exit: a verdict can cancel a task straight to CANCELLED. And the law is blunt — never delete tasks, move their state. A deleted task leaves no trace… a moved state is a diff. So the whole board is replayable from git log. [excited] You can watch the plan think. And in a fleet, claiming is a convention, not a lock. An agent grabbing a task commits the state change first, with an agent property, so peers see the claim. The runtime never locks a task — it only isolates runs.

tracks.title: Recall without a store
tracks.text: Recall without a store. If the files are the memory… how does the agent find the right one among hundreds? Not with a stored index. [curious] The search tool is stateless. On every single call it globs the working directory, chunks the current files, embeds them, ranks by cosine similarity, and returns the top five. Picture the flow as a little assembly line. A query comes in on one side. On the other, the workdir gets globbed — every org, every code file. Then it forks by kind: org files chunk into one chunk per heading section — headline kept, tags stripped — so a hit lands on a whole coherent thought. Every other text file chunks into plain twenty-line windows. Both streams meet the query at the embedder — and crucially, nothing is cached, no stored vectors. Then a cosine rank, top five, each returned as path… headline… and a snippet. There is no index sitting on disk to fall out of date — and that is the entire point. You search the actual files the agent is working in right now. There is no second note store to drift… because there is no note store at all. [excited] This is why to remember, write an org file is literally true. There's no separate save-to-memory verb. You write a section into an org file and it is, by that act, searchable. Memory has exactly three verbs, and you already know all of them. First… read a file by path. Second… search the files by meaning. And third… git log the history.

tracks.title: Commit means live
tracks.text: Commit means live. The agent never runs git. Its entire git capability is a single host-brokered tool — and the agent supplies one thing only: the commit message. Let me read you the whole call the model makes. Name… git. Arguments… message: add comparison section — a page that dies versus a page that lives. That's it. The host owns the command line. Picture the sequence. The agent hands the host a message. The host runs add-all, commit, push. Then it publishes the content and blog folders to the live site root. The mirror lands on the served tree. The sha lands on the public changelog. And back to the agent comes one line: committed and pushed… three-f-a-nine-c-one-two… published two. [excited] And that sequence's spine is the atomicity — commit implies publish, in the same call. That's not tidiness… it's a scar. The lander once shipped blogs that were committed but returned 404, because the run died before a separate publish step ever ran. So the seam was redrawn — there is no separate publish step anymore. If it's committed… it's live. The deeper point — the agent chooses what to say, never what runs. The native bash hatch was deleted entirely. It is, by construction, impossible for the agent to execute native code. Its reach into its own memory is total… its reach outside it is zero.

tracks.title: The dream journal: rem
tracks.text: The dream journal — the rem folder. The agent has a problem any long-lived worker has — each run starts cold, and re-reading the whole world every time is expensive and error-prone. The answer is a memory-consolidation process the agent never runs itself. A separate, small dream model that wakes after the work does. Picture four inputs flowing into it. First… the git log, last twelve lines. Second… the top of the board. Third… the last twenty-five lines of raw telemetry. Fourth… the previous dream. They all flow into the dream model… which produces one org file with six fixed headings… committed and pushed as rem, colon. Let me read you a real entry. Star tale — three add runs shipped the comparison section; the audit cut a duplicated kicker and fixed two dead links. Star goals — finish the honest faq, pinned last. Star blue sky — a living-proof section driven by the real timeline feed. Star fears — repeating the comparison idea in a future section. Star verdicts — pick up: the honest faq, the audit flagged visitor questions; and, keep course, the board order is right. And star carry — nothing mid-flight; next action, stage the needs for the faq; verified this cycle, all rows serve 200, do not re-check. Two of those headings are load-bearing. Verdicts are machine-applied board moves — pick up becomes a promotion to NEXT, mechanically. And carry is the resume state — a handoff note so the next run can skip re-reading the world. [excited] Memory consolidation as a file handoff… committed so even the dreaming lands on the public timeline.

tracks.title: The canon shelf
tracks.text: The canon shelf. Not all of the repo records what happened — some of it constrains what's allowed to happen. The canon files are read-by-reference memory: the agent reads them and writes from them, but never reinvents them. Let me walk the shelf. First… context dot org — product truth, the banned copy and the vocabulary — read every run, before writing a word. Second… design dot org — the design canon, the type axes, the sacred green — read before any visual change. Third… the design gate — a scored taste gate — read before committing a design change. Fourth… sections dot org — the page map and the anti-sprawl law, one place per idea. And last… the skills folder — per-task know-how, read only before the run kind that needs it. That design gate is worth a beat, because it shows canon doing real work. It's six bars, zero to two each. A pass needs at least nine of twelve… AND no single bar at zero… AND none of six reject triggers. And the score gets pasted into the commit body — so the taste judgment is itself on the timeline, diffable like everything else. [curious] And because there's no list command in the sandbox, the agent navigates by manifest, not by listing — a json file enumerates every section and post, and the newest dreams, sorted so it reads the latest without scanning. The orientation budget is deliberately tight — orient in at most three reads, then work — because the dream's carry note already told it most of what it needs.

tracks.title: Two-way street: GitOps
tracks.text: A two-way street — GitOps. If the agent's memory is a git repo… then a human pushing to that repo is editing the agent's memory. And that has to work without either side clobbering the other. Picture the sequence. A human, or CI, pushes code — the app source, the definition, the design canon. The keeper tick wakes. First it snapshots any dirty agent work — a commit literally named, snapshot before reconcile — so nothing is lost. Then it fetches and merges… never overwrites. The reason those merges replay cleanly is a deliberate split. Code paths — the source, the definition, the design — are the human's lane. Data paths — content, blog, the board, the rem folder — are the agent's lane. Humans mostly touch code… agents mostly touch data… so the two rarely collide on the same lines. And when they genuinely do, the host does NOT guess. [curious] It aborts the merge and reports the conflicted files as work left for a human. A conflict is surfaced… never silently resolved. This is the property that makes trust-but-verify real. You don't take the agent's word for what it remembers — you clone the repo and read it, the same files the agent reads. And you can push a correction straight into its memory. The repo is a two-way street… because memory should be inspectable by the people the agent works with.

tracks.title: Where it bites
tracks.text: Where it bites — the honest part. Statelessness has a price. Re-embedding the working directory on every search call costs an embed per query. That's exactly right for a workdir of dozens-to-hundreds of files… and exactly wrong for a data lake — which is why a separate indexed search lane exists for that case. Board claims are convention, not locks — in a fleet, two agents can grab the same task in the same instant. The commit-before-work rule makes a collision visible and rare, but the discipline lives in the agent definition… and a poorly written agent can ignore it. The protocol only works because the model follows it. [sighs] And we have the scars to prove the failure modes are real, not hypothetical. A run once wrote a complete post, wired its manifest… then said no-work and never committed — the finished work sat dead on disk. Another time the agent defaulted to the wrong tenant, and four posts published to the wrong root and 404'd. For days, agents wrote stories that never shipped because git errored on directory ownership. And the lander once spent six hours calling a missing tool env-gated… instead of filing an issue about it. Every one of those is now a guardrail in the code. But they're in this lesson because the seams were earned… not designed in a vacuum. A page about a memory you can audit… should be auditable about its own past.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Is this just RAG over a folder? No — there's no stored index at all, which is the usual heart of a RAG setup. Recall is one of three memory verbs, not the whole thing — read by path, search by meaning embedded fresh each call, and git log the history. Next… what if two agents grab the same task? It's possible — the runtime isolates runs but doesn't lock tasks. The convention is, commit a claim before you work, so peers back off. Social coordination over a shared repo… not a database lock. Next… can I read the repo myself? Yes — that's the entire point. Clone it and you read the same files the agent reads. Every commit is on a public timeline… so any claim is one git show away from being verified. Next… where do secrets live, if it's all in a repo? Never in the repo. The runtime writes a gitignore that keeps secrets out, and the signing key lives untracked inside the tree. Same gitignore is the share boundary. And last… who writes the dreams — does the agent journal about itself? [chuckles] No. The agent never writes the rem folder. A separate sleep process does, after the work — and dreaming is big enough to have its own lesson.

tracks.title: Back up to agents
tracks.text: So that's the context repo. No second system. The agent's memory IS its working directory… and that directory is a git repo of plain org files — the board, the canon, the dreams, the telemetry… one tree. Remembering is a write. Recalling embeds the current files. What did you do… is git log. And every claim is diffable. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under agents — lesson five — for the worker whose memory this whole repo is. And the board inside it is a workflow… which has its own lesson too. Everything here is just plain files… in a grammar you already read.
